text: The board mandated a zero-trust pilot, not an enterprise rollout, and that distinction is the first real decision Mara has to make. Attempting identity, network, and device controls everywhere at once, in 90 days, on a fixed budget, would produce something shallow everywhere instead of something real anywhere.

Mara and CISO Howard Okonjo evaluate candidate boundaries against three questions: what's the blast radius if it fails, how contained is it today, and can it realistically be finished in 90 days. Riverbend's OT and SCADA systems, which run an actual substation and water treatment, sit on the same flat network as general corporate traffic today. That combination of highest stakes and lowest containment makes it the clear pilot target.

The scope statement is deliberately narrow: segmenting the Riverbend OT and SCADA systems into their own zone, a consolidated identity view limited to who can reach that boundary, an automated Python inventory of that access, and a risk-register entry for every finding. Just as important, the document names what's explicitly deferred, like enterprise-wide zero-trust access and a full identity audit, so the deferral reads as a decision, not a gap.

That scoped document is what lets Okonjo defend the plan to the board if anyone asks why Hartwell didn't fix everything at once. Next lesson starts the real inventory work: mapping exactly how identity is spread across Azure AD and AWS IAM before anything gets consolidated.
